summary:
Connecticut is one of fifteen states placed in the 'Most Protective' tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition. The assessment finds Connecticut's laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

State law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in public places, public and private employment, governmental services and the receipt of goods and services; gender identity or expression was added to these protections in 2011. Connecticut's hate-crime statute covers gender identity or expression and carries additional penalties; that legislation was consolidated and strengthened by a law signed in June 2026, effective 1 October 2026.

Connecticut operates a healthcare shield or refuge law, in force since 2022, which protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal here has been banned in the patient's home state. This is directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a state that prohibits gender-affirming care.

Since 1 October 2015, under H.B. 7006, the sex marker on a Connecticut birth certificate can be changed without surgery, on a notarised applicant affidavit plus a notarised affidavit from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist stating appropriate clinical treatment such as hormone therapy. The change followed a 1 June 2015 Senate vote of 32-3 sending the bill to Governor Dannel P. Malloy, replacing the prior requirement for sex reassignment surgery. Driver's licences and state IDs can have their sex designation changed on request, and Connecticut birth certificates, IDs and driver's licences all offer M, F and X markers.

A federal judge dismissed in April 2021 the 2020 lawsuits that had sought to block transgender female athletes from competing in Connecticut girls' high school sports, leaving their eligibility intact.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 ranking contrasts Connecticut's tier with the worst-law states, which carry prison terms of up to five years for gender-identity-based offences in Idaho and arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use in Florida.

Connecticut's healthcare shield law sits within a national picture in which 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states and 5 territories, covering 56%, hold none. Youth-care bans are tracked nationally, with some permanently blocked in court.

Connecticut decriminalised consensual same-sex sexual activity effective 1971, with the age of consent set at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation and lowered to 15 in 1975, and has banned discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in public places, employment, governmental services and receipt of goods and services since 1991. A bill passed in June 2023 to reform the 1991 definition was pending governor action at the time of sourcing.
localsOnly:
Since 1 July 2018 all individuals held in Connecticut custody are treated consistent with their gender identity, including for strip searches and access to clothing, commissary items and educational materials, as well as for housing based on recognised gender.

State anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and expression, explicitly covering cyberbullying and harassment, and applies across all school premises.

Connecticut banned conversion therapy on minors effective immediately on signing in May 2017, after House passage 141-8 on 2 May and Senate passage 36-0 on 10 May. The gay panic defence was repealed after unanimous passage in June 2019, signed by Governor Ned Lamont and effective 1 October 2019.

State hate-crime law also protects on the basis of sexual orientation with additional penalties, under the same June 2026 consolidation effective 1 October 2026.
outOfScopeNotes:
The June 2023 bill to reform Connecticut's 1991 sexual-orientation discrimination definition was described in the source as pending governor action; whether it has since been signed is unresolved in the inventory.

The inventory does not document any Connecticut-specific incident of anti-trans violence, enforcement of the hate-crime provisions, or any state-level facility or bathroom restriction, so no such finding can be stated either way.

Whether Connecticut's shield law has been tested against a specific out-of-state prosecution, and how state authorities respond to federal document or entry rules for visitors, are not sourced here.
